The rollup header shows `total_wall_clock_ms`/busy/wait and highlights + scroll-focuses (`#slowest`) the slowest step. Runs > 500 steps truncate with a note. The nondeterminism-block runbook is surfaced as non-clickable `code` text (a repo path, not a served URL — matching the `docs/runbooks/safe-deploy.md` convention), never a dead relative `<a href>` that would 404 during triage. **Deferred #739/#690 data gaps (honored, not patched with a UI-side history parse)** Per both issues' "file the gap against the data API, never patch in the UI" clause, four ACs are honored only to the extent the shipped derivations expose data, each recommended as a #739 follow-up: (1) per-span deep-links (#960 AC7) — a `TimelineStep` carries no child/activity exec_id; (2) adjacent-attempt spans (#960 AC3) — a step has an `attempt` count but no per-attempt timestamps, so retries render as one span + `×N` badge; (3) historical/resolved pause windows (#960 AC4) — `StepKind` has no `Pause` variant and the row keeps only the active pause; (4) interactive axis zoom (#960 AC8) — deliberately no-JS, min-span-width compression only. Analogously, #957 AC3's "link to underlying task/activity detail where one exists" is honored by the "where one exists" conditional (the #690 `DagRunNode` carries no per-node exec_id, so no link target exists). **Tests** Pure `ui.rs` render tests (status fill/icon/label coverage, `build_graph_layout` levels, SVG nodes/edges/fills/glyph embedding, `render_dag_node_panel`, `node_retry_offered` matrix, `resolve_dag_run_selection`, `dag_detail_relative_url` encoding, timeline lanes/`span_segments`/`x_scale`/rollup/slowest/pause-band/nd-marker/HTML-escaping, step-cap) run under `cargo +1.97.0 test -p autumn-harvest-plugin --lib` (582 passed). `tests/ui_integration.rs` testcontainers tests (mixed-status graph, node detail, retry confirm/commit/audit/admin-gate, classic-DAG + unknown-run degraded, 220-node timed render, real `dag_skip` skipped-node distinctness, index alignment; timeline four-affordance fixture, split-only-when-present, slowest highlight, in-flight open span, 404, 200-step timed render) are compile-checked and run Docker-backed in CI via the registered `ui_integration` suite. Multi-angle review: 0 P1, ~6 P2 all fixed (`run`-param redirect encoding, dead ND-block runbook links → code text, untested 100-node perf metric, unexercised pending-vs-skipped, unasserted status-icon-in-render, unknown-run silent-fallback → 404).
- **Phase 4** (implemented): Scoped API tokens + rotation for the management API — see issue #942. Adds a first-class, least-privilege credential layer for the Harvest management API: create / list / revoke scoped, optionally-expiring, individually-revocable API tokens, with every mutating operation attributable to a named actor. Entirely a `autumn-harvest-plugin` auth layer plus **one additive config-table migration** — **no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, zero replay-determinism impact, no change to `harvest_events`** (AC9). The deterministic execution core is untouched. **What shipped** **Token table (`harvest_api_tokens`, migration `20260713000000`)** — a small, Postgres-only, shard-agnostic control table (`id`, `name`, `token_hash`, `scope`, `created_at`, `expires_at?`, `last_used_at?`, `revoked_at?`, `created_by`), mirrored into core `schema.rs`/`models.rs` exactly like `harvest_audit_log`. Verified on the **default (control) shard**; rows carry no `shard_id`. **Wire format & secret hygiene (AC2)** — a token secret is opaque `hvst_<base64url(32 random bytes)>`. Only `token_hash = hex(SHA256(secret))` is stored (UNIQUE-indexed); the plaintext is returned **exactly once** at creation and never persists. Verification hashes the presented secret and does one indexed `SELECT` — **no in-Rust hash comparison** (a 256-bit random hash is not an iterable timing oracle), so no constant-time-compare crate is added. `GET /admin/tokens` returns a **metadata-only** `TokenView` DTO that structurally cannot hold the hash/secret (the #695 redaction-view pattern, exhaustive-destructure guard); `MintResult`/`NewApiToken` redact the secret/hash in `Debug`. Uses `sha2`/`base64`/`rand` — all already workspace/core deps. **Scope from route classification (AC3/AC4)** — a token carries `read` or `mutate`, derived from the existing `audit::CLASSIFIED_ROUTES` (the #776 single source of truth — **no second route taxonomy**). The scope gate is `deny_readonly_mutation` over `classify_route`, which **fails closed**: an unclassified path resolves to `Mutating` and is denied to a `read` token. A `read` token gets **403 on 100% of `ALL_MUTATION_ROUTES`** and reaches 100% of read-only routes (the 100%/0% success-metric sweep). **Enforcement layer (`api_token::enforce_token_scope`)** — a `from_fn_with_state` layer installed on the nested `harvest_api_router` **only** under the new `HarvestPlugin::enable_api_tokens()` opt-in (default off → byte-identical, AC7). A bearer that does not start with `hvst_` (or an absent bearer) is passed through untouched — token auth **composes with**, never replaces, `api_with_auth` (AC7). A claimed `hvst_` bearer that cannot be verified (store unavailable) is rejected 503, never trusted unverified. **Rotation & expiry (AC5)** — optional `expires_at`; an expired or revoked token is rejected 401 on the **next request** because there is **no grant cache** (every request re-queries the table; bounded TTL = 0). Rotation is create-replacement → cut over → revoke old, over the existing routes. **Actor attribution (AC6)** — on a verified token the layer strips any inbound `x-harvest-actor` and injects `token:{id}`, so every audited mutation is attributed to the token (never the secret/hash) and a caller cannot spoof a different actor. The `token:` audit-actor namespace is **reserved**: on the pass-through path (no/invalid `hvst_` bearer, incl. OPTIONS) the layer also strips any inbound `x-harvest-actor` whose value starts with `token:`, so a caller admitted by some *other* means (a session admin, or any request under an embedder admin boundary) cannot forge a token-namespaced actor and impersonate a minted token. Non-`token:` actor values pass through untouched — legacy embedder-authed requests keep the documented `x-harvest-actor`/`anonymous` fallback. A verified `TokenPrincipal` extension lets `require_harvest_admin` admit a token-authenticated request in standalone-token mode. **Routes (AC1)** — `POST /admin/tokens` (create, 201, audited `token.create`), `GET /admin/tokens` (list, metadata-only, read/no-audit), `DELETE /admin/tokens/{id}` (revoke, audited `token.revoke`), all admin-gated and registered across every registry: `harvest_api_router`, `management_api_routes()`/`_request_fields()`/`_response_fields()`, `docs/api-contract.json`, and core `audit` (`CLASSIFIED_ROUTES`, `ALL_MUTATION_ROUTES`, `AUDITED_OPERATIONS`, `OP_TOKEN_CREATE`/`OP_TOKEN_REVOKE`/`TARGET_TOKEN`, `EXCLUDED_ROUTES` for the GET), with a dedicated `token_routes_are_classified_and_audited` pin. **MCP composition** — a token-aware `enforce_token_scope_mcp_mutation` layer (mirroring `enforce_read_only_mcp_mutation`) is provided in `api_token` to hard-deny a `read`-scoped token the mutating generated MCP tool routes. `enable_api_tokens()` installs the management-router `enforce_token_scope` layer; wiring the MCP-tool gate onto the app-level generated tool routes is a follow-up composition (the generated MCP routes live outside the nested management router). **CLI (AC8)** — `harvest token create|list|revoke` (plus a `rotate` client-side convenience that mints a replacement via the create route). The `--token` bearer was already sent; the new layer consumes it. **Single source of truth for hashing** — the pure token-secret helpers (`mint_secret`, `hash_secret`, `looks_like_harvest_token`, `TOKEN_PREFIX`) live in **core** (`autumn_harvest::api_token`, no `db` feature — they use only the non-optional `base64`/`sha2`/`rand` core deps). The plugin's mint route re-exports and calls them, and the offline `harvest token bootstrap` CLI calls the same functions, so the server mint path and the offline seed path can **never drift** on how a secret is generated or hashed. `sha2`/`base64`/`rand` were removed from the plugin's own `Cargo.toml` (they now live only in core). **First-token bootstrap — standalone (tokens-only) mode** **The problem (Codex P1).** In pure standalone mode — where scoped API tokens are the *only* auth, with no embedder `api_with_auth` admin boundary — there is a chicken-and-egg gap: `POST /admin/tokens` is an admin-gated mutation, so minting a token requires an admin `TokenPrincipal`, which only a *previously-minted* token can provide. There is no way to mint the **first** token via the API. (Composed mode — tokens layered on the embedder's own admin auth — is unaffected: an existing admin caller mints the first token normally.) **The fix — `harvest token bootstrap` (offline seed CLI).** A new local-only CLI subcommand generates a fresh token, prints the plaintext secret **exactly once** (same "shown once — store it now, it cannot be recovered" framing as the create route), and prints the exact `INSERT INTO harvest_api_tokens (...) VALUES (...)` statement for the operator to run against their database out-of-band. It opens **no** DB connection and issues **no** HTTP request (print-only). The printed SQL embeds **only the hash** (never the secret), with `id`/`created_at` taking the column defaults (`gen_random_uuid()`/`NOW()`) and every user-supplied string single-quote escaped (`'` → `''`) to neutralize injection through a crafted `--name`/`--created-by`. `--expires-at` is validated as RFC 3339 before any SQL is emitted. `--scope` defaults to **mutate** (a seed token must be able to mint the rest via the API). Usage: `harvest token bootstrap [--name <name>] [--scope mutate|read] [--expires-at <rfc3339>] [--created-by <who>]`. The operator (who already has DB access — the trust anchor) runs the printed SQL once to seed a single `mutate` token, then mints every further token through the API. **Why option (a) — offline seed CLI — over the alternatives.** (a) keeps **zero new server-side auth surface** and anchors trust in the DB access the operator already has (the same trust anchor the migration itself requires), leaving composed mode byte-identical. A server-side bootstrap secret (b) would add a *static, long-lived credential* the operator must provision, guard, and eventually rotate — a standing liability for a one-time ceremony. A docs-only "insert a row by hand" note (c) would ship an advertised standalone mode that is effectively unusable out of the box and would force operators to hand-derive the `hex(SHA256(secret))` hash correctly (the exact drift hazard this feature removes). The CLI reuses the shared core hashing helper, so a bootstrap-seeded token authenticates **byte-for-byte identically** to a route-minted one — proven by a dedicated parity integration test. **`last_used_at` is debounced** — the best-effort last-used bump runs off the request critical path (fire-and-forget) **and** is skipped when the token's `last_used_at` is newer than 60 s, so a high-rate token client (the intended CI-fleet case) does not turn every read into a write or double the pool-checkout pressure. **Operational caveats** **Standalone-token mode should sit behind a rate-limiting proxy.** With `enable_api_tokens()` as the *only* auth (no reverse proxy / `api_with_auth`), any request whose `Authorization` begins with `hvst_` triggers one indexed token lookup before authentication — inherent to any bearer-token scheme. In that deployment shape, front the management API with a reverse proxy / load balancer that rate-limits (per-source) to bound unauthenticated lookup floods; the lookup is a single cheap indexed `SELECT` per probe and the connection is released promptly, but the mitigation is deployment-level. **Incident response for a compromised `mutate` token must audit `created_by` lineage.** A `mutate` token can reach `POST /admin/tokens`, so it can mint replacement tokens (the 2-level read/mutate model has no scope that grants mutation but withholds token management — fine-grained RBAC is explicitly out of scope). Revoking a leaked `mutate` token is therefore insufficient on its own: also audit the `created_by` provenance and revoke the entire lineage of tokens the compromised token minted. **Tests** Pure unit tests (core `api_token.rs`): hash determinism/hex, secret mint prefix/entropy, minted-secret-round-trips-through-hash, `hvst_` discrimination. Pure unit tests (plugin `api_token.rs`): `MintResult`/`TokenView` redaction, the scope-from-class decision (deny-mutating / allow-readonly / fail-closed), expiry predicate (exercising the re-exported core helpers). Audit pin (`audit.rs`). No-DB HTTP layer tests (`security.rs`): pass-through of absent/non-`hvst_`/OPTIONS, 503-on-claimed-token-without-store, default-router-unchanged. DB integration (`token_auth_integration.rs`): create-returns-secret-once/stores-only-hash, list-metadata-only, verify-authenticates, unknown-401, revoke-denies-next-request, expired-401, the read-token 403/read sweep, mutate-token standalone admin access, `token:{id}` actor attribution (spoof-proof on the token path), a pass-through anti-spoof test proving a non-token caller cannot forge a `token:`-namespaced audit actor (AC6, reserved-namespace strip), create/revoke audited, plus the **bootstrap parity test** (`bootstrap_seeded_token_authenticates_identically_to_route_minted`): proves the mint route stores exactly `hash_secret(secret)` and that a row seeded offline with the shared core helpers authenticates + audits as `token:{id}` identically to a route-minted token. CLI unit tests (`token_bootstrap_tests` in `lib.rs`): builder emits a `hvst_` secret + hash-only INSERT SQL (secret never embedded), default scope `mutate`, invalid-scope rejected, flag-values flow through, RFC-3339 expiry validated/embedded, single-quote escaping. CLI mapping + contract-coverage tests.
- **Phase 5.0** (implemented): `autumn-harvest-sqlite` companion crate — see issue #1068. New workspace member `autumn-harvest-sqlite`: an embedded, single-writer **SQLite** backend for the workflow engine, targeting edge / local-first deployments. It productizes the R&D feasibility spike (issue #966 / PR #1066) into a real crate following the separate-companion-crate recommendation (option ii) — the Postgres path is **completely untouched**. **What it reuses vs. reimplements.** The crate depends on `autumn-harvest` with `default-features = false`, pulling in only the pure, backend-neutral determinism core (`run_workflow`, `WorkflowEvent`, the replay engine, `WorkflowContext`) — no Diesel/Postgres. It reuses that core **wholesale** (the decision loop calls the pure `run_workflow_with_state_history_policy_and_caps(...)` entry point with plain values — no connection, no trait object — threading the real registered `workflow_name` so `ctx.info().workflow_type` matches the Postgres worker; see the FIX C entry below) and reimplements only *persistence* on `rusqlite` (`bundled`, so no system SQLite and **no Docker** for tests): the event store (`store.rs`), the task queue + durable timers (`queue.rs`), and the worker pass (`worker.rs`), wired by `SqliteRuntime` (`runtime.rs`). **No in-crate `StorageBackend` trait** — the core is already reusable as a library. **Single-writer / single-server contract** (documented in the crate docs): `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` replaces `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (exactly-once by construction under one writer); polling replaces `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`; restart = drop the runtime + re-open the file, with an orphan-reclaim on `open()` flipping any crash-stranded `RUNNING` task back to `PENDING` (activity execution is **at-least-once** — bodies should be idempotent). Durable timers use the **real wall clock**: a timer's absolute deadline (`now + duration`) is stored at arm time, so timers are naturally monotonic across restarts with **no virtual clock to persist or reset**; the public drivers use `Utc::now()`, and `*_as_of(now)` variants inject an as-of time so restart/timer tests are deterministic without sleeping. **The load-bearing correctness work — decision-cycle persistence atomicity as a CLASS invariant.** The spike prototype left the append-then-mutate ordering non-transactional (an open Codex P1). Every persist site in this crate wraps its event append(s) **and** its durable-row mutation(s) in ONE `conn.transaction()`, so a crash (or a mid-write drop) can never leave the event history and the durable rows observably out of sync across a reopen: **start** — execution-row insert + `WorkflowStarted` append. **dispatch** — the whole decision cycle's `ActivityScheduled`/`TimerStarted` appends + task/timer row inserts (a mid-batch unsupported command rolls the whole cycle back — no half-written cycle). **drain** — the activity body runs *outside* the transaction (a SQLite write lock cannot be held across arbitrary user I/O — hence at-least-once), but the terminal `ActivityCompleted`/`ActivityFailed` append + task-row completion (or the retry requeue + attempt audit) commit together. **timer fire** — `TimerFired` append + mark-timer-consumed in one transaction (a crash between them would otherwise double-fire the timer and leave a stray non-lifecycle `TimerFired` in history). **signal delivery** — `SignalReceived` append + the `harvest_signals` delivered-flag update ride the same cycle transaction. **terminal** — `WorkflowCompleted`/`WorkflowFailed` append + execution-state → terminal in one transaction. The cycle's drained bookkeeping commands (see below) are appended **before** the terminal event, in command order, inside that same transaction (mirroring the Postgres worker's `persist_terminal_outcome_commands`); any non-bookkeeping command in a terminal drain is rejected loudly with `SqliteError::Unsupported`, rolling the whole terminal transaction back. **bookkeeping** — a `RecordSideEffect` command (from `ctx.system_now`/`new_uuid`/`random_*`/`side_effect`) is persisted as a `SideEffectRecorded` event, and `RecordMarker` as `MarkerRecorded`, **never silently dropped** — whether it rides a suspending batch (via `apply_commands`) OR is emitted in the cycle that completes/fails the workflow with no further suspension (e.g. `ctx.new_uuid()` right before `Ok(..)`, persisted on the terminal path above). Both cases join the same atomic cycle transaction, so replay never re-mints a different value and a history written here always replays byte-identically on the core `WorkflowReplayer`. `ctx.set_current_details(...)` (issue #593) and a re-park `WaitForActivity` are benign **no-ops** (they append no event and gate no control flow) rather than `Unsupported` errors, so a workflow that publishes an operator status breadcrumb is not wedged. **timer re-arm** — a timer id may be RE-ARMED under the same name after a prior fire (the poll-loop idiom `loop { ctx.timer("tick", 1).await?; … }`, which the core supports via cursor-based per-id FIFO pairing). Arm idempotency keys on OCCURRENCE (`store::pending_timer_arms` = recorded `TimerStarted` minus `TimerFired` for the id), NOT the bare id, and `enqueue_timer` uses `INSERT OR REPLACE` so the fresh arm supersedes the spent (`fired = 1`) row — a bare-id guard would wrongly match the prior fired arm and wedge the re-arm at `Stuck`. **Determinism / cross-backend guarantee.** A history written here is byte-identical **per event** to one the Postgres backend would write (both serialize `WorkflowEvent` via the shared adjacently-tagged `#[serde(tag = "type", content = "data")]` form), so it replays unchanged on the core `WorkflowReplayer` — including a deterministic side effect emitted in a terminal (completing/failing) cycle, which is now persisted (see the terminal/bookkeeping bullets above). The claim is *per-event encoding byte-identity + replay-equivalent event SETS*, not identical event streams: the Postgres engine appends an `ActivityStarted` on claim that this backend never writes, and the two replay identically because `HistoryMatcher::scan_activity_terminal` skips `ActivityStarted`. Retryable activity failures go to a `harvest_activity_attempts` audit table + the task-row `attempt` counter (mirroring the Postgres `requeue_for_retry`), so only terminal outcomes ever reach the replayable event log. **Signals are pull-only (documented non-goal).** A staged signal reaches history (`SignalReceived`) only when a workflow reaches a pull primitive that consumes it. The supported pull surface is the plain waits (`ctx.wait_for_signal` / `ctx.receive_signal`) **and** the signal-or-deadline waits `ctx.wait_for_signal_timeout` / `ctx.receive_signal_timeout` (issue #476) — see the Codex #1069 P2 fix below. The push-handler and non-blocking drain APIs — `register_signal_handler` (#546), `drain_signals` / `try_receive_signal` (#775) — depend on the Postgres task-preparation ingest that promotes *all* pending signals into history up front, which this single-writer backend does not implement; restrict to the pull primitives here (push-based signal *handlers* are a follow-up). **Codex #1069 review — P2: handle `CancelRaceLosers` so `wait_for_signal_timeout` completes.** A workflow using `ctx.wait_for_signal_timeout(...)` / `receive_signal_timeout(...)` suspends on a `StartTimer` + `WaitForSignal` race. When the **signal wins**, the determinism core pushes a `WorkflowCommand::CancelRaceLosers { timers: [<deadline timer>], .. }` (issue #476/#600) to durably delete the losing deadline timer. Both command-drain sites — `apply_commands` (a teardown riding a suspending batch) and `persist_terminal_pending_commands` (the common `let s = ctx.wait_for_signal_timeout(..).await?; Ok(s)` terminal-drain shape) — previously treated it as `SqliteError::Unsupported("Unknown")`, so *after* `SignalReceived` was already committed the next cycle errored and the execution could never complete — wedging every normal pull-style signal workflow that adds a timeout. Both sites now delegate to a shared `apply_cancel_race_losers` (mirroring the Postgres `worker::apply_race_loser_cancellations`): it deletes each losing timer's still-pending `harvest_timers` row (new `queue::delete_pending_timer`, returning whether a row changed so the idempotent re-push on later replay cycles reports no progress and the decision loop still converges) and, for a race over activities, cancels each losing still-open task row (new `queue::cancel_activity_task`) and appends the synthetic `ActivityFailed { error: "lost race to a sibling branch", non_retryable: true, .. }` the core records — only for a row it actually cancelled, so an activity that genuinely completed first keeps its real terminal. All teardown joins the same cycle transaction (atomic with the winner/terminal event). A non-empty `children` set (a child-workflow race — `StartChildWorkflow` is outside the single-writer subset, so it can never have been dispatched here) is still rejected loudly rather than silently dropping a loser the core would cancel. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no schema change** (the `CANCELLED` task state is terminal for the claim query, which only selects `PENDING`). Regression tests (`tests/signal_timeout.rs`): signal-wins completes with the payload and the losing deadline timer row is actually deleted (verified via a raw connection) and the history replays on the core `WorkflowReplayer`; deadline-wins returns the timeout branch (`None`); and a typed `receive_signal_timeout` with a trailing activity exercises the suspending-batch (`apply_commands`) site. The two signal-win tests fail against the pre-fix code and pass after. **Codex #1069 review — P1: engine non-determinism must NOT seal FAILED / poison history.** When replay detects workflow-code drift (a bad deploy), the determinism core returns `WorkflowOutcome::Failed { non_deterministic_details: Some(_) }`. The `drive_one_cycle` terminal `Failed` arm previously ignored that field and persisted a normal `WorkflowFailed` event + `FAILED` state — sealing an engine bug as an author failure and poisoning history against the rolled-back build. The arm now branches on `non_deterministic_details`: `None` (a genuine author `Err`) fails terminally, unchanged; `Some(_)` (an engine-detected divergence) **discards the whole divergent decision cycle** — appends NO terminal event, persists NONE of the cycle's pending bookkeeping commands (a marker from the bad build would poison history), and does NOT transition state — leaving the execution `RUNNING`/resumable and surfacing the new `SqliteError::NonDeterministic { execution_id, details }`. Because the `?` never runs, `harvest_events` is byte-identical to before the drive; a later drive with a corrected (compatible) handler resumes from the same unchanged history and completes. Propagating the error out of the drive also terminates the decision loop, so `run_until_blocked`/`poll_once`/`run_until_idle` cannot spin — the operator fixes/rolls back and re-drives. This is the minimal-correct mirror of the Postgres engine's issue #603 gate (which additionally does an automatic block-with-backoff — a documented follow-up here). Regression test (`tests/runtime_robustness.rs::engine_nondeterminism_is_nonterminal_and_resumable`): a phase-1 workflow arms a durable timer (records `[WorkflowStarted, TimerStarted]` and blocks); flipping an injected drift flag makes the SAME workflow schedule an activity at that command slot; re-driving the unchanged history surfaces `NonDeterministic`, appends NOTHING (no `WorkflowFailed`, history byte-identical, execution still `RUNNING`), and after restoring the compatible build the run resumes and completes — plus `author_error_still_seals_failed` pins the `None` arm. Both fail against the pre-fix code (the drive returns `Ok(RunState::Failed)`). **Codex #1069 review — P2: an unregistered-activity claim is released, not stranded.** `queue::claim_next_ready_task` commits a task to `RUNNING` *before* the worker resolves its handler; if the activity name has no registered body, the drain previously returned `UnregisteredActivity` with the row left `RUNNING` — invisible to later drains (which only re-claim `PENDING`) until a full DB close+reopen ran the orphan reclaim (`UnregisteredActivity → Stuck` until a reopen). `drain_ready` now RELEASES the claim back to `PENDING` (new decrement-free `queue::release_claim`, guarded on `state = 'RUNNING'`, consuming no attempt and not advancing `run_at` — the body never ran) before surfacing the error, so a later drain re-claims it once the body is registered in the SAME runtime, no reopen. Regression test (`unregistered_activity_releases_claim_and_is_reclaimable`): after the error the task row is `PENDING` (verified via a raw connection), and registering the body + re-driving completes the workflow — fails pre-fix (task stranded `RUNNING`). The pre-existing `durability.rs::orphaned_running_task_is_reclaimed_and_body_reruns` test used the unregistered-activity path to *fabricate* a stranded-`RUNNING` orphan; it now fabricates that genuine crash-BEFORE-finalize state directly (raw `UPDATE ... SET state = 'RUNNING'`), keeping its real orphan-reclaim / at-least-once intent intact. **Codex round 8 — activity-panic containment.** A registered activity body that `panic!()`s (rather than returning `Err`) would unwind past the finalize/requeue branch AFTER the task row is already `RUNNING`, so no failure/requeue ever commits and the run wedges permanently (the claim query only re-selects `PENDING`; a single-process design has no live-peer poison-pill net). `drain_ready` now wraps the body invocation in `std::panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(...))` and converts a caught panic into the crate's NORMAL retryable-activity-failure path — treated exactly like `Err(msg)`: `finalize_activity_result` records the attempt and follows the retry policy (requeue if attempts remain, else terminal `ActivityFailed`). `AssertUnwindSafe` is sound (the body ran outside any transaction; on a caught panic its result is discarded). Mirrors the Postgres worker's handler-panic containment (issue #782), using the shared `autumn_harvest::error::panic_message` extractor. Regression tests: `panicking_activity_is_contained_and_exhausts_to_terminal` (a body that always panics, `max_attempts = 2` → both attempts caught+recorded → terminal `ActivityFailed`/`WorkflowFailed`, task never stranded `RUNNING`) and `panicking_activity_retry_then_succeeds` (panic on attempt 1, succeed on attempt 2 → the workflow completes, no terminal `ActivityFailed` in the log, the panic recorded only in the per-attempt audit). Both fail pre-fix (the panic unwinds through the tokio test). **Codex round 8 — mixed timer + activity batch.** A single decision cycle emitting BOTH a `StartTimer` and a `ScheduleActivity` (`tokio::join!`) is dispatched correctly: `apply_commands` already appends a cycle's schedule events in COMMAND order (a `for cmd in commands` loop), so **no drain-order change was needed** — the Codex "went Stuck" symptom is a poll-order concern, not a schedule-order one. Regression test (`mixed_timer_activity_batch_completes_and_replays`): with the activity as the first joined future (`join!(activity, timer)`), the batch dispatches both, the activity completes, the run blocks cleanly on the still-armed timer (not Stuck), a later drive fires the timer, the workflow completes, the two schedule events are in command order, and the resulting history replays byte-identically on the core `WorkflowReplayer` — proving the core matcher tolerates the interleaved sibling terminals (`ActivityCompleted` then `TimerFired`). **Documented CORE limitation (not a backend bug):** the REVERSE order — `join!(timer, activity)`, the timer polled first — is unsupported by the *core* determinism engine itself. `HistoryMatcher::match_timer_strict` (replay.rs) breaks its forward `TimerFired` scan at an unconsumed `ActivityScheduled` (it skips consumed siblings, child workflows, signals, external, update, and cancellable-timer events, but stops on an unconsumed activity); verified directly — the core `WorkflowReplayer` rejects even an ideal timer-first history with `NonDeterminismDetected(EarlyCompletion)`. This is shared with the Postgres engine and out of scope for this backend to change; put the activity branch first in a mixed `join!`. On this backend a timer-first mixed batch does not silently loop forever — the driver's `MAX_ITERATIONS` bound surfaces `SqliteError::Stuck` — but it is not a supported shape. **Codex #1069 review (commit `524823a`) — P1: a late signal must not beat an expired timeout.** When a workflow is parked in `wait_for_signal_timeout` / `receive_signal_timeout`, the decision cycle consumed any staged signal (`apply_commands`'s `WaitForSignal` branch, previously `store::take_pending_signal`) BEFORE `worker::drain_ready` appended the due `TimerFired` later in the same cycle. If the deadline passed while the runtime was idle and a signal arrived AFTER that deadline but before the next poll, history recorded `SignalReceived` first, so the timeout wrongly resolved as an approval — even though the core models a late signal as `TimerFired` **then** `SignalReceived` (so the late signal remains observable to a later plain wait). Fixed by mirroring the Postgres `merge_wake_events` arrival-time ordering: `harvest_signals` gains a `received_at` epoch-second column (set by `stage_signal`; a new doc-hidden `send_signal_as_of(exec, name, payload, now)` seam injects it deterministically, paired with the `*_as_of` drivers, while `send_signal` uses the wall clock). The `WaitForSignal` branch now delegates to `worker::ingest_awaited_signal`, which peeks the oldest pending signal's `received_at` and, via `queue::due_timers_before_signal`, fires every due deadline timer whose `fire_at <= received_at` **first** (ties to the timer, matching `received_at < fires_at` ⇒ signal-first), then appends the `SignalReceived`; a due timer whose deadline is *after* the signal arrived is left for the ordinary `drain_ready` pass to fire *after* the signal, so an on-time signal still wins even when the run is only driven past the deadline. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant** (this is a brand-new crate, so the additive column needs no migration). A plain `wait_for_signal` (no deadline timer) and any wait driven before its deadline are unchanged — a pending signal only ever interleaves with a deadline timer that is already *due* at drive time, so the three pre-existing `signal_timeout.rs` tests (which deliver before the deadline) are unaffected. Regression tests (`tests/signal_timeout.rs`): `late_signal_does_not_beat_expired_timeout` (signal delivered after the deadline → the run resolves `auto_rejected`, `TimerFired` precedes the still-recorded `SignalReceived`, and the history replays on the core `WorkflowReplayer`) and `on_time_signal_still_wins` (signal delivered before the deadline but driven past it → the approval wins, `SignalReceived` precedes the later-fired `TimerFired`). The first fails against the pre-fix ordering (the late signal wins). **Codex #1069 review (commit `524823a`) — P1: a workflow-handler panic must not seal FAILED on the first strike.** `run_workflow_with_state` distinguishes a caught **workflow-handler** panic (`Failed { handler_panic: true }`, distinct from an activity-body panic — that already had containment) from an author `Err`. The `drive_one_cycle` terminal `Failed` arm treated it like an author `Err(...)`: it appended `WorkflowFailed` and sealed `FAILED` on the FIRST strike, permanently closing a transiently-panicking or hotfix-able run. A new gate — placed beside the non-determinism gate, BEFORE any terminal side effect — now contains it (issue #782 analog). A per-execution consecutive-panic strike counter (`SqliteRuntime.workflow_panic_strikes`, in-process, cleared on any non-panic outcome so only *consecutive* panics count) is bounded by the new `WORKFLOW_PANIC_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3` const (mirroring the Postgres worker's default). Under budget the panicked cycle is **discarded** — no terminal event appended, none of its (already-empty) pending commands persisted, state stays `RUNNING` — and surfaced as the new `SqliteError::WorkflowPanicked { execution_id, details }`, which propagates out of the drive loop (mirroring the non-determinism gate) so a hotfix/rollback can re-drive the UNCHANGED history to completion; only at/over budget is the run sealed with the typed `HandlerPanic` error (as a normal `RunState::Failed`). A genuine author `Err(...)` carries no panic flag and still fails terminally on the first strike, unchanged. Regression tests (`tests/runtime_robustness.rs`): `workflow_handler_panic_is_not_sealed_on_first_strike` (a workflow whose body always `panic!()`s stays `RUNNING` with no terminal event under budget and seals `WorkflowFailed` only after the budget is exhausted — never on the first strike) and `workflow_handler_panic_then_hotfix_resumes` (panic on the first drive, flip an injected hotfix flag so the corrected handler completes → the run completes `42`, and the history is exactly `[WorkflowStarted, WorkflowCompleted]`, proving the panicked cycle persisted nothing). Both fail against the pre-fix code (sealed on the first strike). **Codex #1069 review (commit `524823a`) — FIX C: thread the real `workflow_name` into the executor (cross-backend fidelity).** The decision loop called `run_workflow_with_state(exec, history, handler, input, empty_shared_state(), None)` — the trailing `None` is span-metadata, so the core built the `WorkflowContext` with an EMPTY `workflow_name` (the `workflow_name` param that populates `ctx.info().workflow_type`, issue #698, is separate from `span_meta.workflow_name`, which feeds only the OTel span this backend has no worker for). A workflow that used the documented replay-safe `ctx.info().workflow_type` — in an activity input, an idempotency key, or a branch — therefore recorded/replayed `""` here while the Postgres worker injects the real handler name: a divergence on the very byte-identity guarantee the crate makes. Fixed by driving through the pure, already-`pub` caps-carrying entry point `executor::run_workflow_with_state_history_policy_and_caps(...)`, passing the registered `workflow_name` (available from the execution row) in the dedicated load-bearing parameter and reproducing `run_workflow_with_state`'s own defaults for every other argument (`WorkflowHistoryPolicy::default()`, no declarative handlers, the `DEFAULT_MAX_*`/`DEFAULT_CURRENT_DETAILS_CAP_BYTES` caps, empty context headers, no offload, `NoOpMetrics`; `span_meta` stays `None`). **No core change** — the entry point and the cap consts were already `pub`. Regression test (`tests/cross_backend.rs::workflow_type_reaches_ctx_info_and_replays_on_core`): a workflow reads `ctx.info().workflow_type`, routes it through an activity input, and returns it — the run completes with the real registered name (NOT `""`), the recorded activity input carries it, and the history replays `ReplaySucceeded` on the core `WorkflowReplayer`. Fails pre-fix (records/returns `""`). **Codex #1069 review (commit `1e346f1`) — P2: `send_signal` rejects unknown / terminal targets.** `send_signal` staged a signal row unconditionally, and `harvest_signals` has no FK/state check, so a typoed `ExecutionId` or a signal to an already-`COMPLETED`/`FAILED` run returned `Ok(())` while the wakeup was silently lost — no live pull primitive (`wait_for_signal` / `receive_signal[_timeout]`) will ever consume it. `send_signal` (via `send_signal_as_of`) now validates the target BEFORE staging, mirroring the Postgres `signal::send_signal` rejections (and the crate's own `outcome()` not-found pattern): an unknown id → `SqliteError::ExecutionNotFound`; a terminal execution (per `autumn_harvest::erase::is_terminal_state`) → the new `SqliteError::WorkflowNotRunning { execution_id, state }`; a `RUNNING` execution stages (and later consumes) the signal exactly as before. The single-writer runtime holds SQLite's only write handle, so the state read and the stage cannot race a concurrent transition. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no schema change.** Regression test (`tests/runtime_robustness.rs::send_signal_rejects_unknown_and_terminal_targets`): an unknown id → `ExecutionNotFound` with zero staged rows; a `COMPLETED` execution → `WorkflowNotRunning` with zero staged rows; a `RUNNING` execution stages and drives to completion consuming the payload. The two rejection cases fail against the pre-fix code (which returned `Ok(())` and staged an unconsumable row). **Codex #1069 review (commit `1e346f1`) — P2: "fire expired timers before draining activities" assessed and DECLINED (a replay regression for the only reachable shape).** The finding proposed reordering `worker::drain_ready` to fire due `TimerFired` events *before* running ready activity bodies, so an activity-vs-timeout race that is only driven past the deadline records the deadline first. This was implemented, tested end-to-end, and **reverted**: for the *only* mixed activity+timer suspension expressible in this crate's subset — `tokio::join!(activity, timer)` with the activity polled first (the documented "Codex round 8 — mixed timer + activity batch" shape; the reverse order is already an unsupported core limitation) — the reorder produces a history the **core** determinism engine cannot replay. The core's `HistoryMatcher::scan_activity_terminal` (replay.rs) skips `TimerStarted`/`TimerCancelled` mid-scan but **breaks its forward `ActivityCompleted` scan at an unconsumed `TimerFired`** (`_ => break`), so `[…, TimerFired, ActivityCompleted, …]` leaves the activity permanently in-progress → the run wedges at `SqliteError::Stuck`. Verified directly on the core `WorkflowReplayer`: the current (activity-first) drain order `[…, ActivityCompleted, TimerFired]` replays `ReplaySucceeded`, while the finding's proposed order `[…, TimerFired, ActivityCompleted]` replays `NonDeterminismDetected`. The finding's premise ("replay resolves the activity branch even though the deadline passed") presupposes an order-tolerant activity-vs-timeout **race** matcher (the analog of `match_signal_or_timer`, which is why the sibling late-*signal* ordering fix in `ingest_awaited_signal` is sound); no such matcher exists for activity+timer, and `ctx.race()` explicitly rejects a mixed activity+timer shape (`HarvestError::Config`, pinned by the core's own `race_rejects_mixed_activity_and_timer_shape`). Correcting the finding would require a core change to `scan_activity_terminal` (out of scope — no `autumn-harvest/src/` changes) plus a new activity-vs-timer race primitive — far beyond a minimal faithful fix. The current drain order is therefore left unchanged. **Durability & concurrency pragmas.** `open()` sets `PRAGMA synchronous = FULL` (fsync on every commit — the conservative durability the crash-then-reopen tests rely on), `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` (the idiomatic single-writer + occasional-reader embedded choice; a harmless no-op on an in-memory database), and `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` (a second connection racing the writer's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` claim retries briefly instead of failing instantly with `SQLITE_BUSY`). WAL + FULL is fully durable. `run_until_idle()` returns the new `SqliteError::Runaway` when the fleet driver never quiesces within its iteration safety bound, rather than swallowing it as a clean `Ok(())` a caller could not distinguish from genuine quiescence (mirroring `run_until_blocked`'s `Stuck`). **No import/seed API** — the cross-backend guarantee is export-shaped (a SQLite-produced history → the core `WorkflowReplayer`) and needs none; a future edge → hub ingest path that rebuilds derived task/timer rows from open scheduled work (or rejects such histories) is a follow-up. **Public API.** `SqliteRuntime::open(path)` / `open_in_memory()` (reopen-safe — all state in the DB), `register_workflow(&WorkflowInfo)`, `register_activity(&ActivityInfo, body)` (the audited, declared-default-driven path — the analog of `register_workflow`) / `register_activity_raw(name, ActivitySpec)` (the hand-made escape hatch, no audit — the analog of `execute_activity_raw`), `start_workflow(name, input) -> ExecutionId`, `send_signal(exec, name, payload)`, `poll_once()` / `run_until_idle()` / `run_until_blocked(exec)` (+ `*_as_of` test seams), `load_history(exec) -> Vec<WorkflowEvent>`, `activity_attempts(exec, name)`, and the `outcome(exec)` accessor. Typed `SqliteError`/`SqliteResult` (thiserror). `RunState` / `ExecutionOutcome` / `ActivitySpec` / `ActivityBody` / `ActivityAttempt` are re-exported. **Known limitations (documented):** a crash *mid activity body* leaves the task `RUNNING` and is recovered by the reclaim on next `open()` (re-running the body — at-least-once); a single-process design has no live-peer heartbeat/poison-pill reclaimer, by design. Signals are pull-only (see above). The `activity_attempts(exec, name)` audit accessor is name-scoped: a workflow scheduling the same activity *name* more than once returns a single merged, attempt-ordered list across those instances (`load_history` remains the per-instance source of truth). (The former "deterministic side effect in a completing cycle is dropped" limitation is **fixed** — see the terminal/bookkeeping bullets above.) **Tests (no Docker; `rusqlite` bundled):** 8 inline unit tests pinning the atomic rollback/commit of each dispatch/drain/timer-fire site; a **reopen-consistency sweep** (`tests/reopen_consistency.rs`) that drives one workflow through every persist-site type (start → side effect → activity dispatch+drain → timer arm+fire → signal → terminal), reopens the DB at each stage, and asserts history ⟷ durable rows are always consistent (no scheduled event without its task row, no terminal event with a still-pending row, no fired timer left unmarked, execution state matches the terminal event) plus the activity body running exactly once across all reopens; durability scenarios (`tests/durability.rs`: activity retry-then-success, timer fires across restart, signal delivery, deterministic replay after a crash-AFTER-commit not re-executing the activity, and orphaned-RUNNING reclaim re-running the body after a crash-BEFORE-commit); cross-backend replay (`tests/cross_backend.rs`: a SQLite history replays on the core `WorkflowReplayer`, per-event JSON byte-stability, a hardcoded GOLDEN encoding assertion, PG-shaped-history event-SET equivalence, and a frozen `ctx.new_uuid()` side effect persisting across a reopen and replaying byte-identically); and a review-hardening suite (`tests/review_fixes.rs`: terminal-only + after-last-suspension side effects persist and replay, `set_current_details` does not wedge completion, activity retry-exhaustion → `ActivityFailed`/`WorkflowFailed`/`Failed` outcome, direct `Err` return fails terminally, an unsupported mid-batch command rolls the whole cycle back, a re-armed timer id fires again across a reopen, and `run_until_idle` drives multiple executions). CI gains a `Clippy autumn-harvest-sqlite` step (lint job) and a `cargo test -p autumn-harvest-sqlite` step (test job); the `msrv` `cargo check --workspace` auto-covers compile. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no core-crate changes, no migration — the Postgres path is byte-unaffected.** The crate depends on the pure core surface only; `rusqlite 0.38` (`bundled`, `libsqlite3-sys 0.36.0`) unifies with the existing dependency graph. **Codex #1069 review (commit `48d54b2`) — P2: a deterministic tie-breaker for equal timer deadlines.** `queue::due_timers` (and its signal-interleave sibling `due_timers_before_signal`) ordered due rows by `fire_at` ALONE, so two timers armed with the same deadline — e.g. `tokio::join!(ctx.timer("a", 1), ctx.timer("b", 1))` — fired in SQLite's *unspecified* tie order. If the backend appended `TimerFired(b)` before `TimerFired(a)` while the `join!` polls `a` first, the run's history no longer replays: the core `HistoryMatcher::match_timer_strict` (replay.rs) scans forward for its OWN `TimerFired`, skipping interleaved `TimerStarted`/`TimerCancelled` siblings, but **STOPS (`break` → `NoMatch`) at an unconsumed sibling `TimerFired`** of a different id. Verified empirically on the core `WorkflowReplayer`: a history that fires in `TimerStarted`-append order `[…, TimerStarted(a), TimerStarted(b), TimerFired(a), TimerFired(b), …]` → `ReplaySucceeded`, while the reversed fire order `[…, TimerFired(b), TimerFired(a), …]` → `NonDeterminismDetected(EarlyCompletion)`. Unlike the DECLINED activity-vs-timer reorder finding above (the core has no order-tolerant activity-vs-timer matcher, so *no* fire order replays — a genuine core limitation), timer-vs-timer with equal deadlines IS replayable by the core **provided the fire order equals the arm order**, so this is a genuine, in-subset BACKEND fix. `harvest_timers` gains a monotonic `arm_seq` column (`MAX(arm_seq) + 1` at arm time, assigned in `enqueue_timer`; robust to `VACUUM`, unlike an implicit `rowid`; a re-arm via `INSERT OR REPLACE` correctly gets a fresh higher value), and both due-timer queries order by `(fire_at, arm_seq)` — so equal-deadline timers fire in `TimerStarted`-append (= command/poll) order, which is exactly what the core requires. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant; the additive column needs no migration (brand-new crate).** Regression tests: two `queue.rs` unit tests (`due_timers_break_equal_deadlines_by_arm_seq` — rows inserted so arm order is the reverse of rowid order, asserting arm-order output on both due-timer queries; `enqueue_timer_assigns_monotonic_arm_seq_including_on_rearm` — strictly increasing `arm_seq` in call order, and a re-arm gets a fresh higher value) and two integration tests (`tests/review_fixes_48d54b2.rs`: `equal_deadline_timers_fire_in_arm_order_and_replay_on_core` — the money test, a SQLite-driven `join!` of two same-deadline timers fires `[a, b]` and the history replays `ReplaySucceeded` on the core; `reversed_timer_fire_order_breaks_core_replay` — the falsifiable control proving a reversed hand-built fire order breaks core replay, i.e. why the `arm_seq` tie-break is load-bearing). (SQLite's `ORDER BY fire_at`-only tie order is genuinely unspecified — it may coincide with arm order or not — so the unit test pins the deterministic guarantee and the reversed-history control carries the hard-falsifiable proof.) **Codex #1069 review (commit `48d54b2`) — P2: honor the activity's declared/per-call retry policy.** A typed `ctx.execute_activity(&info, …)` / `execute_activity_with_opts` call carries the activity's resolved `RetryPolicy` in the core `WorkflowCommand::ScheduleActivity::retry_policy_override`, but `apply_commands` DROPPED that field (`ScheduleActivity { .., .. }`) and the task row had no place to persist it, so `worker::drain_ready` decided retries solely from the registered `ActivitySpec::max_attempts`. A call that DECLARED retries (`#[activity(retry = …)]` or a per-call `execute_activity_with_opts` override) could therefore fail after ONE attempt, or a call that DISABLED retries could be retried — depending purely on how the body happened to be registered. Fixed by threading the declared cap end-to-end: `harvest_tasks` gains a nullable `max_attempts` column; the `ScheduleActivity` arm extracts `retry_policy_override.as_ref().map(|p| p.max_attempts)` and `persist_scheduled_activity` → `queue::enqueue_activity` persists it; `ClaimedTask` carries it back through `claim_next_ready_task`; and `drain_ready` uses `task.max_attempts.unwrap_or(spec.max_attempts).max(1)` — the declared per-call cap WINS, and the raw `execute_activity_raw` path (which carries `retry_policy_override: None`) still falls back to the registered `ActivitySpec` default byte-for-byte. Only `max_attempts` is honored: this backend models no retry *backoff* (a requeue runs at `run_at = now`), so the policy's delay fields have no surface here; the load-bearing attempt cap is honored. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant; the additive column needs no migration (brand-new crate).** Regression tests (`tests/review_fixes_48d54b2.rs`), each constructed so the registered spec and the declared override DIFFER (proving the override wins in BOTH directions): `declared_retry_policy_raises_attempts_over_registered_spec` (registered `ActivitySpec::new(1, …)` = no retry, declared `RetryPolicy::fixed(4, …)`, body fails 3× then succeeds → the workflow COMPLETES with exactly 4 attempts; fails pre-fix, capped at 1); `declared_retry_policy_disables_retries_below_registered_spec` (registered `5`, declared `1`, always-failing body → fails after EXACTLY ONE attempt; fails pre-fix, runs 5); and `raw_path_without_override_uses_registered_spec_default` (the raw path with a 3-attempt spec still exhausts 3 attempts — the fallback is unregressed). **Codex #1069 review (commit `6de2d8b`) — P2: sub-second (millisecond) timer deadlines, so a timer never fires early.** The `*_as_of` / wall-clock drivers passed `now.timestamp()` (whole SECONDS) into the arm calculation, flooring the arm instant before adding `duration_secs`: a `duration = 1s` timer armed at `…000.900` stored `fire_at = …001` (whole second), so a poll at `…001.001` fired it after only ~100 ms — ~900 ms EARLY — violating "a durable timer never resolves before its deadline", and the same truncation could flip an on-time signal past its `wait_for_signal_timeout` deadline near a second boundary. Fixed by carrying every internal epoch value at **millisecond** precision: the three `DateTime<Utc> → i64` seams (`run_until_blocked_as_of`, `poll_once_as_of`, `send_signal_as_of`'s `received_at`) now use `now.timestamp_millis()`, and the `StartTimer` arm computes `fire_at = now_ms + duration_secs * 1000` (checked mul then add; a pathological duration saturates to `i64::MAX` instead of overflowing). `fire_at`, `received_at`, and `run_at` are all relative epoch-milliseconds, so the whole comparison (`fire_at <= now`, `fire_at <= received_at`) stays self-consistent — **no DDL change** (the columns are already `INTEGER`) and no reachable behavior change for the whole-second durations every other timer/signal test uses (a uniform ×1000 scaling: `t0` and each `chrono::Duration::seconds(n)` delta scale together). Regression tests (`tests/subsecond_timer.rs`): `timer_armed_at_fractional_second_does_not_fire_early` (arm a 1 s timer at `…000.900` via the `_as_of` seam → the stored `fire_at` equals `t0.timestamp_millis() + 1000`, a poll at `+100 ms` leaves it `WaitingTimer` — NOT fired — and it fires only at the true `+1 s` deadline; fails pre-fix on both the `fire_at` value assertion, `3_000_001` vs `3_000_001_900`, and the early-fire behavioral assertion) and `whole_second_timer_still_fires_at_its_deadline` (a whole-second arm still fires exactly at its deadline and not 1 ms before — no regression for integer durations). **Codex #1069 review (commit `5663be7`) — P2: the public drivers refresh the wall clock PER decision cycle.** The public `run_until_blocked` / `poll_once` wrappers captured `Utc::now()` ONCE and handed that single timestamp to every internal `drive_one_cycle`. Because a cycle can consume real wall-clock time — an activity body runs *between* the cycle that dispatches it and the cycle that arms a follow-up timer — a timer armed in a later cycle was persisted with an absolute `fire_at` relative to the START of the outer call rather than its true arm instant: a `timer(1s)` following a 2s activity stored `fire_at = call_start + 1s`, already ~1s in the past by the time it was actually armed, so it fired immediately on the next poll instead of waiting ~1s from arm time. Fixed by making ONLY the public wall-clock wrappers own their decision loop and re-read the clock at the START of each cycle (a new `SqliteRuntime.now_fn` clock source, default `Utc::now`); the `_as_of` seams are unchanged — they still take a single caller-fixed timestamp and remain the deterministic-simulation surface (tests rely on that fixed clock, so refreshing them would break the injected-time contract). The per-cycle refresh only makes arm times MORE accurate; late-signal ordering (`ingest_awaited_signal`) and the sub-second (millisecond) precision are undisturbed (each cycle still floors to `timestamp_millis()`, now at its true instant). A new doc-hidden `set_clock(now_fn)` seam installs a controllable clock so the public path's per-cycle refresh is asserted deterministically without sleeping. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no schema change, no core change.** Regression tests (`tests/drive_clock_refresh.rs`): `public_run_until_blocked_refreshes_the_clock_per_cycle` (an injected clock returns `t0` on its first read and `t0+2s` on every read after — simulating a 2s activity between cycle 1 and cycle 2 — so a `timer(1s)` armed in cycle 2 anchors to `t0+2s` → deadline `t0+3s`, the driver reads the clock more than once, and a poll at the arm instant `t0+2s` finds the timer still pending rather than firing it immediately; fails pre-fix — a single read collapses the whole call to `t0`, so `fire_at = t0+1s` is already overdue at `t0+2s`) and `timer_armed_after_a_slow_activity_anchors_to_its_arm_cycle_not_call_start` (the deterministic `_as_of` concept lock: driving cycle-by-cycle via `poll_once_as_of` with manually advanced timestamps anchors the later-armed timer's deadline to its arm-cycle `now`, locking the `drive_one_cycle` arm behavior the public per-cycle refresh depends on). **Codex #1069 review (commit `6de2d8b`) — P2: scope the signal-ingest timer reordering to ONLY the raced deadline timer (correct defense; the described end-to-end join wedge is a separate, pre-existing core limitation).** The finding observed that `worker::ingest_awaited_signal` (added by the commit-`524823a` late-signal fix) runs for EVERY `WaitForSignal` command, and its due-timer loop fired *every* due timer whose `fire_at <= received_at` ahead of the `SignalReceived` — so in principle a `join!(ctx.wait_for_signal("go"), ctx.timer("t", 5))` with the signal delivered after `t` is due could record `TimerFired(t)` before `SignalReceived(go)`, which the core `match_signal` cannot skip (it stops at an interleaved `TimerFired`), wedging replay. `ingest_awaited_signal` now reorders ahead of the signal ONLY the raced `__signal_timeout:{seq}:{name}` deadline timer of THIS wait (matched structurally via a new private `is_signal_timeout_deadline_timer` helper — strip the `__signal_timeout:` prefix, `split_once` the seq's colon, compare the remainder to the signal name, so a name containing `:` or a `LIKE` metacharacter still matches exactly, mirroring the core's inline `format!("__signal_timeout:{seq}:{signal_name}")` convention in `autumn_harvest::context`, issue #476). An unrelated durable timer is left for the ordinary `drain_ready` pass to fire *after* the signal, at a history position the workflow's own timer-await consumes. This is the correct issue-#476 semantics (only the raced deadline may beat a late signal) and preserves the existing `wait_for_signal_timeout` race exactly (its sole armed timer IS the `__signal_timeout` deadline timer, so the `late_signal`/`on_time` tests are unaffected). **Honest scope correction:** empirically (verified by driving the runtime end-to-end and by the core `WorkflowReplayer`), the specific `join!(wait_for_signal, timer)` scenario the finding cites is (a) **not resolved by this scoping** and (b) **not a regression from the late-signal fix**. Because a durable timer is always armed at drive time (`fire_at = now + duration > now`), a due unrelated timer is fired by `drain_ready` in an *earlier* drive iteration than the one in which the workflow's replay re-emits `WaitForSignal` (on replay the recorded `TimerStarted` makes the independent `match_signal`/`match_timer` branches suspend in different iterations), so `ingest_awaited_signal` never actually sees an unrelated due timer to over-fire — the timer-first history (and the resulting `WaitingSignal` wedge) is produced by `drain_ready`, not `ingest`, and predates the late-signal fix. That end-to-end plain-`join!(wait_for_signal, timer)` wedge is the same class of CORE-matcher limitation as the DECLINED "fire expired timers before draining activities" finding above (there is no order-tolerant plain-wait-vs-unrelated-timer matcher; `match_signal` stops at an interleaved `TimerFired`) and is out of scope for this backend to change (no `autumn-harvest/src/` changes). The idiomatic, fully-supported way to bound a signal with a timer remains `ctx.wait_for_signal_timeout` (which works). The ingest-scoping fix is therefore shipped as a correct **defense** (ingest must never over-fire unrelated timers ahead of a signal), demonstrated at the level it actually governs. Regression tests (`src/worker.rs` unit tests): `ingest_reorders_only_the_raced_deadline_timer_ahead_of_the_signal` (seed a staged signal plus BOTH a raced `__signal_timeout:0:go` deadline timer and an unrelated `t`, both due before the signal, then call `ingest_awaited_signal` → ONLY the deadline timer fires, ahead of the signal; the unrelated `t` stays unfired; fails pre-fix, which also records `TimerFired(t)`, `["t", "__signal_timeout:0:go"]` vs `["__signal_timeout:0:go"]`) and `signal_timeout_deadline_timer_predicate_matches_only_the_raced_timer` (the name predicate: matches `__signal_timeout:{seq}:{name}` including a colon-bearing name, rejects a wrong name, an unrelated timer, and a prefix look-alike). **Codex #1069 review (commit `926fb6a`) — P2: preserve typed workflow-failure metadata (cross-backend byte-identity, AC5).** When a `#[workflow]` returns a typed `WorkflowFailure` (issue #767) — and when the workflow-panic budget is exhausted, whose `error` is the encoded `HandlerPanic` envelope — the macro shim encodes the failure into a `harvest_workflow_failure_v1` wire envelope carried on the failure string. The Postgres terminal path DECODES that envelope (`crate::failure::decode_workflow_failure`) and writes `WorkflowFailed` with the typed `error_type`/`details` (+ the human message), storing the human `decoded.message` in the execution `error` column. `drive_one_cycle`'s terminal `Failed` arm (and the panic-budget-exhausted path in `contain_workflow_panic`) previously persisted `WorkflowEvent::workflow_failed(error.clone())` and stored the RAW envelope in `harvest_executions.error` — so a SQLite history for a typed failure was NOT byte-equivalent to a Postgres one (the `error_type`/`details` were `None`, and the `error` column held the wire envelope). Both sites now DECODE before appending/updating, exactly as the Postgres path does: the `WorkflowFailed` event is built with `WorkflowEvent::workflow_failed_typed(&decoded)` (typed `error_type`/`details` preserved), the execution `error` column holds `decoded.message` (never the raw envelope), and `RunState::Failed` surfaces the human message. The typed test fails against the pre-fix code (the surfaced value is the raw `{"harvest_workflow_failure_v1":…}` envelope and `error_type`/`details` are `None`). **Codex #1069 review (commit `926fb6a`) — P2: honor the activity's `start_to_close` timeout, and CLOSE the dropped-`ScheduleActivity`-field class.** The core `WorkflowCommand::ScheduleActivity` carries `start_to_close_override` (from both `execute_activity_with_opts` and `ActivityInfo::default_start_to_close`), but `apply_commands` DROPPED it (`ScheduleActivity { .., .. }`), so a slow registered body ran to completion and recorded `ActivityCompleted` instead of `ActivityTimedOut` — diverging from the durable event the Postgres timeout scanner records. Because a synchronous body cannot be cancelled mid-flight in a single-writer runtime, this is a **post-execution outcome**: the recorded HISTORY is byte-equivalent even though the wall-clock behavior (the body runs to completion before the timeout is recorded) differs. Replay-safe: the outcome is recorded once and replay never re-runs the body, so a body whose timing varies across a crash-rerun cannot diverge a committed history. **This closes the whole "dropped `ScheduleActivity` field" class** — every author-declared field on the command is now HONORED (`activity_id`/`name`/`input`/`queue`; `retry_policy_override` → `max_attempts`, prior commit; `start_to_close_override`, this commit) or REJECTED LOUDLY (`session_id`/`session_worker_id`, worker sessions #606; the session-acquire-only `schedule_to_start_override`) — none is silently ignored. it has no surface in this single-writer backend (activities drain inline, so there is no claim delay to enforce) and is a documented non-goal. **Codex #1069 review (commit `9e480b8`) — P2: honor the WHOLE retry policy (backoff timing + non-retryable classification), superseding the `max_attempts`-only fix from `48d54b2`.** The prior commit persisted only the declared `max_attempts`, dropping `initial_interval`/`backoff_coefficient`/`max_interval` (backoff timing) and `non_retryable_errors`; Fixed by persisting the whole policy and honoring it in the worker: `harvest_tasks` gains a nullable `retry_policy_json TEXT` column (the additive companion to `max_attempts`); the `ScheduleActivity` arm serializes `retry_policy_override` (`serde_json::to_string`) and `persist_scheduled_activity` → `queue::enqueue_activity` persists it; `ClaimedTask` carries the deserialized `Option<RetryPolicy>` back through `claim_next_ready_task`; and `worker::finalize_within_tx` uses it. **Backoff:** a retryable failure with attempts remaining is requeued at `run_at = now + compute_retry_delay(initial_interval, backoff_coefficient, max_interval, attempt_num)` (the shared core helper, `attempt_num` 1-based so the first retry waits `initial_interval`) — a future `run_at` that `claim_next_ready_task` (`run_at <= now`) will NOT re-claim until the driver advances the clock, so the workflow BLOCKS on the backing-off activity (the driver's `classify_block` now returns `RunState::WaitingTimer` for a `PENDING` task via the new `queue::has_pending_activity`, so a poll before the deadline neither re-runs the body nor spins to `Stuck`). a non-retryable failure fails terminally on the first attempt regardless of `max_attempts`, preventing side-effect repetition. **No core export needed** — `policy::compute_retry_delay`, `RetryPolicy::is_non_retryable`, and `failure::parse_typed_payload` are all already `pub` and reachable under `default-features = false`. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant; So `worker::ingest_awaited_signal` compared the WRONG arrival time against a `wait_for_signal_timeout` deadline: a LATE signal staged first + an ON-TIME signal staged second let the timeout win (the late signal's `received_at` was past the deadline) and marked the late row delivered while the on-time row stayed queued. Because a body can consume real wall-clock time before returning `Err`, a `RetryPolicy::fixed(60s)` body that failed 45s in scheduled its next attempt only ~15s after the actual failure (or *immediately* if the body ran longer than the delay) — unlike the Postgres path, which computes the delay AFTER handling the result. The wall-clock drivers (`run_until_blocked`/`poll_once`) pass a closure that re-reads the runtime's `now_fn` clock seam (a cheap `Arc` clone captured once, so it never borrows `self` across the `&mut self` cycle call); the `_as_of` drivers pass one returning the caller-fixed epoch, so `failure_now() == now` and deterministic simulation is byte-identical to before (the existing `retry_policy_backoff_delays_the_requeue` `_as_of` test is unchanged). **A ZERO computed delay is an IMMEDIATE retry requeued at the CYCLE-START `now`** — covering both the raw `execute_activity_raw` path (`retry_policy == None`) AND a zero-interval policy (`RetryPolicy::fixed(n, 0ms)`) — so it re-claims in the same drain pass and the retry sequence converges in one call (anchoring an immediate retry to `failure_now`, which is `>= now` under the wall clock, would defer it past the drain pass and make `run_until_blocked` return `WaitingTimer` early — a regression the pre-existing wall-clock `declared_retry_policy_raises_attempts_over_registered_spec` 0ms-policy convergence test catches). Jitter exists to de-synchronize a FLEET of concurrent workers; this backend is single-writer / single-server (there is no fleet to de-synchronize — activities are drained one at a time under one write lock and one polling driver), so the base delay is behaviorally equivalent, and retry timing (`run_at`) is not recorded in `harvest_events`, so honoring or not honoring jitter has ZERO replay / byte-identity impact.
